summary: Defines an extension to SCTP that lets a host add or remove IP addresses on an existing association without tearing it down. SCTP is built to use multiple network addresses for resilience, and this lets the set of addresses change as interfaces come and go. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine you are on a call and get a second phone number. This lets you add or drop numbers during the call without hanging up, so the conversation keeps going.

questions: can sctp add ip addresses dynamically
how does sctp add an ip address
can sctp change addresses without restarting
subtitle: How an SCTP association adds, removes and re-prefers IP addresses while it keeps running.

tldr.problem: SCTP associations can use several IP addresses for fault tolerance, but the address set was fixed at startup. Adding a network card or renumbering a network meant restarting the association, which many fault-tolerant applications treat as an outage.
tldr.mechanism: Two new chunks, ASCONF and ASCONF-ACK, carry Add IP Address, Delete IP Address and Set Primary Address requests to the peer. They are authenticated, sent one at a time, and acknowledged with correlation IDs.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can change their addresses mid-association. The price is a strict set of rules and a requirement for SCTP authentication, because address changes are a way to hijack an association.

today: RFC 5061 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4960 and depends on the chunk authentication of RFC 4895.

sections.title: Why Addresses Need to Change
sections.content:
A host can have several points of attachment to the Internet. RFC 4960 SCTP was built to use such a multi-homed host for fast failover and for an association that survives hardware failures.

But modern computers allow hot-pluggable network cards, and in IPv6 a provider can renumber a network. Before this extension, using a new or renumbered address meant restarting the transport association, which many fault-tolerant applications consider an outage.

This RFC lets an SCTP stack dynamically add an IP address to an association, dynamically delete one, and ask the peer to use a particular address as primary. It also adds a small 32-bit adaptation indication that can be exchanged at startup so the right layer below the application can be enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, if you got a new phone number you would have to hang up and call again. This makes it possible to share the new number without ending the call.

sections.title: The ASCONF and ASCONF-ACK Chunks
sections.content:
Two new chunk types carry the control information reliably. The ASCONF chunk (type 0xC1) holds a 32-bit Sequence Number, a mandatory Address Parameter that names an address of the sender, and one or more request parameters in type-length-value form. The ASCONF-ACK chunk (type 0x80) copies the Sequence Number and carries zero or more results.

Both chunks MUST be sent authenticated with the mechanism of RFC 4895. An unauthenticated one MUST be silently discarded. The upper two bits of the ASCONF type are set, so a receiver that does not understand it skips the chunk and reports an Unrecognized Chunk Type error rather than aborting. The sender then MUST NOT send further ASCONF chunks.

Success is the default. A receiver can report complete success by returning only the chunk header and Sequence Number, with a Chunk Length of 8. Only failures, or optional explicit successes, need parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: An ASCONF is a note saying 'please change my address list'. An ASCONF-ACK is the reply. If everything went fine, the reply can be an almost empty note that just says 'got it'.

sections.title: Parameters and Error Causes
sections.content:
Seven parameters are defined. Inside an ASCONF, Add IP Address (0xC001), Delete IP Address (0xC002) and Set Primary Address (0xC004) each carry a 32-bit ASCONF-Request Correlation ID, an opaque value the receiver copies back unchanged, plus the address. In an ASCONF-ACK, Error Cause Indication (0xC003) and Success Indication (0xC005) carry the matching correlation ID.

Three parameters appear at startup in INIT and INIT-ACK: Set Primary Address, Adaptation Layer Indication (0xC006, passed opaquely to the upper layer) and Supported Extensions (0x8008). An implementation of this extension MUST list the ASCONF, ASCONF-ACK and AUTH chunks in its Supported Extensions parameter.

An address of 0.0.0.0 or ::0 is a wildcard that means the packet's source address. Broadcast and multicast addresses MUST NOT be used.

Five new error causes support the exchange, such as refusing to delete the last remaining address, refusing to delete the packet's source address, a resource shortage, and a request refused for lack of authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request has a ticket number. The reply quotes the ticket number so the sender knows which request it answers, and error replies explain what went wrong.

sections.title: How ASCONF Exchanges Work
sections.content:
The sender gives each ASCONF a Sequence Number, initialized at association start to the Initial TSN and incremented by one for each new chunk. It starts a T-4 retransmission timer. Only one packet holding ASCONF chunks may be outstanding at a time, which stops address changes from flooding the network. Each side can have one in flight, so two may cross on an association.

If the timer expires, the sender updates error counters, doubles the RTO of the destination, and retransmits the same ASCONF with the same Sequence Number. It MAY bundle later ASCONFs with higher Sequence Numbers. Chunks are not sent outside the ESTABLISHED, SHUTDOWN-PENDING, SHUTDOWN-RECEIVED and SHUTDOWN-SENT states, and SHOULD NOT exceed the PMTU.

The receiver processes the TLVs in order, accepts only the next expected Sequence Number, caches its ASCONF-ACK for retransmission, and replies to the source address of the packet that carried the ASCONF. A stale or unexpected Sequence Number is discarded, possibly as an attack. Sequence arithmetic is modulo 2**32.
sections.plainLanguage: You may only have one note waiting for an answer at a time. If the answer is late, you send the same note again, a bit more slowly each time.

sections.title: Rules for Adding, Deleting and Choosing a Primary
sections.content:
An added address is not fully added until the ASCONF-ACK arrives. Until then the sender MUST NOT use it as a source for any packet except one carrying an ASCONF. The receiver may use it as a destination at once but MUST run path verification and send only the ASCONF-ACK or HEARTBEAT chunks to it until verified. Addresses added by an ASCONF start UNCONFIRMED.

A deleted address stays a valid destination for receiving until the ASCONF-ACK arrives and MUST NOT be used as a source afterwards. An endpoint MUST NOT delete its last remaining address, and a request to delete the source address of the carrying packet MUST be rejected. If an Add fails for lack of resources, all later Add or Delete requests in the same ASCONF must fail too.

Because of packet reordering, data can arrive for an address just added or just deleted. For a late packet to a deleted address, an endpoint may hold the address valid, but for no longer than 2 RTO intervals.

Set Primary is advice: the receiver SHOULD honor it, and SHOULD NOT if the address is not part of the association. It can also appear in INIT and INIT-ACK as an initial preference.
sections.plainLanguage: A new number only counts once the other side says 'okay, I have it'. You can never remove your last number, or you would be unreachable.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Adding and deleting addresses gives attackers another way to hijack an association, so the RFC requires the authentication of RFC 4895. Where an attacker could intercept the first two packets of association setup and SCTP-AUTH runs without pre-shared keys, the RFC says authentication MUST use a preconfigured shared endpoint pair key.

Wildcard addresses are a weak spot because the packet's source address is not protected by SCTP-AUTH. An on-path attacker could alter it to add an address of its choice, delete every address but one, or force a primary address. Endpoints that fear on-path attackers SHOULD NOT use wildcards.

An endpoint that gets an INIT announcing ASCONF support without AUTH support MUST send an ABORT or silently discard it, and must never reply with an INIT-ACK. The INIT and INIT-ACK are not protected by AUTH, so an on-path attacker can alter the Supported Extensions parameter, but the RFC argues this adds little beyond what such an attacker could already do. Bombing attacks are covered in RFC 5062.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting someone change the address list could let a stranger sneak into your call. So every change must come with a secret handshake proving it is really the other side.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new chunk types, six parameter types and five new error causes in the SCTP parameters registry. The error cause codes run from 0x00A0 to 0x00A4.

It also creates an adaptation code point registry for 32-bit integers, assigned through IETF Consensus. No initial values are added by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Like giving each new kind of note its own official number in a shared list, so nobody picks the same number twice.
